rashi:a1.1: They and their lots: when they are surrounded by a wall.
rashi:a1.2: But they stand to be dismantled: as was said (above, Arakhin 33b): one does not make them into small villages or large cities.
rashi:a1.3: It might enter your mind: as long as they have not been dismantled, if they sold them before they were dismantled, let them become the buyer’s permanently. It teaches us [that this is not so].
rashi:a2.1: What does the verse teach: “as a field dedicated”: what does the dedicated field come to teach about a field that goes out to the priests in the Jubilee?
rashi:a2.2: His dedicated field: a field that an Israelite dedicated and that came into his share.
rashi:a2.3: Since it goes out to the priests: if he does not redeem it, for it is his like an ancestral field; and now it is in my possession, etc.
rashi:a3.1: I acquire those of others: if an Israelite’s ancestral field were going out to the priests in the Jubilee, I would have a share in it.
rashi:a4.1: Just as the ancestral field of an Israelite: if a priest redeemed it from the Temple treasury, it goes out of his possession in the Jubilee and is divided among all his brothers the priests, as was said in the other chapter, the chapter Ein Makdishin (above, Arakhin 25b). So too this one, etc.
rashi:a5.1: Here he takes it, etc. [Rashi gives only the heading.]
rashi:a6.1: “And every man’s hallowed things shall be his”: we expound this in the chapter HaGozel in Bava Kamma (109b): From where do we know that a priest may come and offer his offerings at any time and any hour he wishes — if he must bring a sin offering, or he volunteered a burnt offering or a peace offering — and he need not give them to the men of the priestly watch, but he himself offers it, takes the hide and eats the meat? The verse states: “And every man’s hallowed things shall be his.”
rashi:a7.1: His hallowed things are not in his possession: and he does not take them by his own right, but because he offers their sacrificial portions.
rashi:a7.2: Here it is in his possession: that is, he would take it by his own right, and not from the table of the Most High as wages for the service.
rashi:a8.1: Rather, Rav Naḥman said: this is why it was necessary to write “dedicated”, for it might enter your mind, etc., that this too is his ancestral field, and if he consecrated it and did not redeem it, it would not go out to the priests in the Jubilee; rather, he would have the right to redeem it forever.
rashi:a8.2: It teaches us: the juxtaposition, by which the dedicated field is juxtaposed to the ancestral field of an Israelite, [teaches] that it goes out of his possession and is divided among the priests. For it is his ancestral field that has redemption forever, but his dedicated field is not like an ancestral field, to be redeemed forever.
tosafot:a1.1: They and their lots stand to be dismantled: And if you ask, what difference does it make if they were dismantled, since they were surrounded by a wall originally? For it was taught above: “that has a wall” — even though it does not have one now, as long as it had one before. Perhaps one can say that this follows Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yosei. And here it is different: since they are fit not to have a wall, the sanctity of the wall that they had before does not help them, and it is as if it had never been.
tosafot:a5.1: Are they comparable? There he acquires: Here too [the Gemara] could have objected that when he acquires the fields of others, it is when it falls during his own priestly watch, whereas here he wants to acquire it [even] for another watch, and it is not divided among the priests of another watch, as explained above (Arakhin 25a). But it raises a stronger objection than that: even if his own watch is serving when it goes out to the priests, he cannot acquire it [all for himself] by this a fortiori inference.
tosafot:a6.1: Rami bar Ḥama said: It was necessary, etc. [Rather,] Rav Naḥman said: [It was necessary;] it might enter your mind, etc. And if you ask: what is it that we said, “and it is a logical inference”? We should not be saying that he acquires it by an a fortiori inference, but because of the verses written: “a man…” [Tosafot’s text reads “when a man consecrates”; the verse Rami bar Ḥama cites is “And every man’s hallowed things”] for Rami bar Ḥama, and “perpetual possession” for Rav Naḥman. One can say: nevertheless, [the baraita] preferred to bring an a fortiori inference like this, from reasoning.
tosafot:a8.1: It teaches us “his ancestral field”: his ancestral field, yes; his dedicated field, no. And if you ask: above we derived it from the juxtaposition, which juxtaposes his dedicated field to the ancestral field of an Israelite, so why does it expound it here from “his ancestral field”? One can say that this is its meaning: it teaches us from “the ancestral field” of the priest that specifically his ancestral field has redemption forever and is not divided among the priests in the Jubilee, but his dedicated field is divided among the priests in the Jubilee, by the juxtaposition that juxtaposes it to the ancestral field of an Israelite, and it is not like his ancestral field, to be redeemed forever. And so Rashi explained.
gershom:a1.1: They and their lots: that is, together with their walls.
gershom:a2.1: And their lots stand to be dismantled: that is, but their walls stand to be dismantled, since one does not make them into either small villages or large cities, and so they still do not have [the status of] houses of walled cities.
gershom:a3.1: Even so, perpetual redemption was necessary. It might enter your mind: before they are dismantled… that is, before they are dismantled, if they are sold, let them become [the buyer’s] permanently. It teaches us perpetual redemption.
gershom:a4.1: His dedicated field: which an Israelite dedicated and which came into the hand of a priest, and he consecrated it and did not manage to redeem it before the Jubilee arrived.
gershom:a5.1: That he may not say: since it goes out to the priests in the Jubilee — for this priest who consecrates his dedicated field is as though he consecrated his ancestral field and did not redeem it, which goes out to the priests in the Jubilee.
gershom:a6.1: Those of others: a field that an Israelite consecrated and did not redeem, which goes out to the priests — I acquire it.
gershom:a7.1: My own, all the more so: that I should acquire it, so that it does not leave my possession.
gershom:a8.1: Just as the ancestral field of an Israelite: which an Israelite consecrated and did not redeem, which goes out from the Temple treasury to the priests in the Jubilee; and if one of the priests redeemed it, it goes out of his possession and is divided among all his brothers the priests, as was said above in the chapter HaMakdish Sadehu: his ancestral field is his, but this one is not his; it belongs to all the priests.
gershom:a9.1: So too his dedicated field goes out and is divided among all his brothers the priests.
gershom:a10.1: Are they comparable? There he merely acquires: for the Merciful One grants him [a share in] the ancestral field of an Israelite that goes out to the priests, together with the other priests.
gershom:a11.1: Here he takes all of it: that is, from whom did he gain [the right] to seize his dedicated field for himself?
gershom:a12.1: Rami bar Ḥama said: It was still necessary, for it might enter your mind that this “and it is a logical inference” is a real inference, since it is written: “And every man’s hallowed things shall be his.” [It is explained in the Sifrei: From where do we know, of an Israelite who was measuring out teruma for a priest on the ground, that any priest who comes there while he is measuring has a share in it like this first one? The verse states: “And every man’s hallowed things shall be his”,] that is, for all of them equally. One might think that even if he had measured it into the basket of the first one, another would acquire [with him]? The verse states: “whatever any man gives the priest, it shall be his” — and not another’s. So it might enter your mind that just as he acquires in sacred things, taking his share with the first priest if he came before it was measured out to him, so that the first one cannot push him away, [so too this dedicated field is like his hallowed things, and no one can push him away, but it should be his. That is why the juxtaposition was necessary.]
gershom:a13.1: Are they comparable — these hallowed things to the dedicated field? Hallowed things are not in his possession but in the Israelite’s possession; the Merciful One [merely] grants them to him. Here, this dedicated field is in his own possession; [and while it is in his possession,] who grants it to him? It is not a valid inference.
gershom:a14.1: It was necessary; it might enter your mind: since it is written “for that is their perpetual possession” — that it returns to him in the Jubilee and does not leave his possession — this dedicated field too is his ancestral field and should not leave his possession. That is why the juxtaposition was necessary: his ancestral field is his, but his dedicated field is not; rather, it leaves his possession and is divided among his brothers the priests. [This is] the wording of my teacher the Gaon. “His hallowed things are not in his possession”: [a note in the printed edition adds:] See Bava Kamma 109, which implies that it speaks of a priest who comes to offer his offerings in a watch that is not his, and nevertheless its service and its hide are his; see there. Perhaps it means that since this verse is adjacent to the verse about robbing a convert, we expound the adjacency, so that this verse too speaks of robbing a convert: for example, a priest who robbed a convert may offer the guilt offering in another watch, and its service and its hide are his. For it establishes this verse as referring to robbing a convert who died, where he pays the principal and the fifth to the priests [and the guilt offering goes to the altar].
gershom:a15.1: We will return to you, “One Who Sells His Field,” and Masechet Arakhin is concluded.
